items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite sitting), passage-final clause; right subject is a part of the obvious noun (the fish’s eyes)
items.passage: The barreleye (Macropinna microstoma), an unusual deep-sea fish found throughout the northern Pacific, has a transparent, fluid-filled shield enclosing the top of its head. Despite sitting deep within this protective canopy, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the barreleye can rotate its two tubular eyes, so it can look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
there are two tubular eyes that can rotate, letting the barreleye look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
the barreleye’s two tubular eyes can rotate, letting the fish look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
the rotation of the barreleye’s two tubular eyes lets the fish look straight up for prey or forward while feeding.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that sits deep within the protective shield on the fish’s head, which can only be the fish’s eyes, not the whole fish. Choice C places “the barreleye’s two tubular eyes” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the eyes.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
A.why_wrong: “The barreleye” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the whole fish sits deep within the shield that covers its own head.

B.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

D.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “rotation,” so the sentence says that a movement, rather than the eyes, sits deep within the shield.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (barreleye fish, Macropinna microstoma, eyes that rotate inside a transparent head shield). No named researchers. Band 7 on the 37e5c794 (3.16) and 2dd1b8bf pattern: the opener fits only a part of the obvious noun, the right subject is a possessive built on that noun, and the hardest distractor (A) starts with the fish and keeps every fact. Options 19 to 21 words; key the shortest.
band7_moves: component key: only the eyes can sit within the shield, so the right subject is “the barreleye’s two tubular eyes,” a possessive built on the obvious noun (as silica glass’s atomic arrangement in 2dd1b8bf)
hardest distractor (A) starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, failing only on what the opener can describe
the key is the only option opening with a possessive, so a student taught that possessive subjects dangle (recipe P) is drawn away from it
key noun (eyes) absent from the passage; recipes W, E, N

band7.why: Component key on the 2dd1b8bf pattern (the barreleye’s two tubular eyes), hardest distractor A starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, plus E and N; key noun absent from the passage. Options run 19 to 21 words, longer than the 12 to 16 the spec suggests, but no option dies on an obvious fact.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Averaged for each location), passage-final clause; right subject is a property (walking speed)
items.passage: In a 1976 study, researchers Marc and Helen Bornstein timed pedestrians walking a fixed distance along the main streets of locations in several countries, ranging from small rural villages to metropolitan areas with populations in the millions. Averaged for each location, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the walking speed of the pedestrians rose steadily with the size of the local population.
the pedestrians walked faster and faster as the size of the local population increased.
the researchers found walking speed to rise steadily with the size of the local population.
there was a steady rise in walking speed as the size of the local population increased.
items.explanation: Only a quantity, such as a speed, can be averaged for each location. Choice A places “the walking speed of the pedestrians” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the speed.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun keeps every fact
B.why_wrong: “The pedestrians” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the pedestrians themselves were averaged for each location.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the researchers
C.why_wrong: “The researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the researchers were averaged for each location.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Bornstein and Bornstein 1976, “The pace of life”: walking speed rose with population size). Real study, known; only its core finding is stated. Band 7 on the fced396a (3.26) and 8b017d4e (3.27) pattern: “Averaged for each location” admits only a quantity, so the key is “the Y of X” while B starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, and C copies the 3.27 move of offering the researchers as subject. Options 14 to 16 words; key not the longest.
band7_moves: property key: only a measured quantity can be “averaged for each location,” so the right subject is “the walking speed of the pedestrians” (the Y of X, as the HHI score of a market in fced396a)
hardest distractor (B) starts with the obvious noun, the pedestrians, and keeps every fact
a second wrong subject (the researchers) that looks like the safe reporting frame of 3.14 and 3.27
fresh opener (Averaged for each location) instead of the officials’ “Compared with that of”; recipes W, W, E

fixes: passage: “psychologists Marc and Helen Bornstein” to “researchers Marc and Helen Bornstein” (Helen Bornstein’s field not confirmed; neutral role word)

band7.why: Property key (“the walking speed of the pedestrians”) on the fced396a and 8b017d4e pattern; B starts with the obvious noun and keeps every fact, C offers the researchers as in 3.27. Run is short (19 words), so it sits at the low end of band 7.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final clause
items.passage: Firefly squid (Watasenia scintillans) spend most of the year at considerable depths in the Sea of Japan, producing bioluminescent light from tiny specialized organs on their bodies. Rising toward the surface by the millions to spawn each spring, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Japan’s Toyama Bay fills with a blue glow from the squid, drawing crowds of visitors to the shore.
the squid’s light organs fill Japan’s Toyama Bay with a blue glow that draws crowds of visitors to the shore.
it is in Japan’s Toyama Bay that the squid create a blue glow, drawing crowds of visitors to the shore.
the squid fill Japan’s Toyama Bay with a blue glow that draws crowds of visitors to the shore.
items.explanation: The squid themselves are what rise toward the surface to spawn. Choice D places “the squid” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the squid.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the place
A.why_wrong: “Japan’s Toyama Bay” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the bay rises toward the surface to spawn.

B.why_wrong: The head of “the squid’s light organs” is “organs,” so the sentence says the light organs, rather than the squid, rise toward the surface to spawn.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (firefly squid spawning in Toyama Bay, Japan). No named researchers. Band 6: plain agent subject, recipes W, P, E; “to spawn” rules out the light organs as well as the bay. Key the shortest option.

band7.why: Plain agent key (the squid), the band-6 R3 pattern; W, P, E distractors, with “to spawn” killing the light organs quickly. Written to band 6.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank; right subject is a part of a building (its roof)
items.passage: Spanish-born Mexican architect Félix Candela specialized in roofs built from hyperbolic paraboloids, saddle-shaped surfaces whose double curvature makes them remarkably strong for their weight. A concrete shell only about four centimeters thick, ______ covers an open dining hall without a single interior column.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Candela’s use of this form at Los Manantiales, a restaurant in Mexico City,
the roof of Los Manantiales, a restaurant Candela designed in Mexico City,
Candela designed Los Manantiales, a restaurant in Mexico City, and its roof
Los Manantiales, a restaurant that Candela designed in Mexico City, has a roof that
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a concrete shell about four centimeters thick, which can only be the restaurant’s roof. Choice B places “the roof of Los Manantiales” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the roof.

A.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
A.why_wrong: The head of “Candela’s use of this form” is “use,” so the sentence illogically says an architect’s use of a shape, rather than the roof, is a concrete shell four centimeters thick.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the person
C.why_wrong: “Candela” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the architect himself is a concrete shell.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the whole building, with the part moved into the predicate
D.why_wrong: “Los Manantiales,” the restaurant, follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the restaurant is a concrete shell four centimeters thick, even as it says the restaurant has a roof; the shell is the roof, not the restaurant.

items.notes: Subject: arts, architecture (Félix Candela’s Los Manantiales restaurant, Xochimilco, 1958, a thin hyperbolic paraboloid shell). Band 6 as WAVE.md directs: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so the planned band 7 is written as a strong band 6. Moves kept from band 7: the right subject is a part of the obvious noun (the roof of Los Manantiales), and two wrong subjects are the building and its architect. Key not the longest. Option D (the restaurant as subject) rebuilt in review on the fced396a pattern (“a less concentrated market will have an HHI score that”): the restaurant “has a roof that” covers the hall, so the sentence itself separates the building from its shell and the opener can only describe the roof.

fixes: option D rebuilt from “Los Manantiales, a restaurant that Candela designed in Mexico City in 1958,” to “Los Manantiales, a restaurant that Candela designed in Mexico City, has a roof that”: the old D was defensible by metonymy (thin-shell buildings are routinely called shells), and the kill leaned on the verb, not the modifier; the new D follows fced396a D and states the roof separately, so only B fits; why_wrong and notes updated

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 with a part-of-building key (the roof) and the whole building as the hardest distractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options; singular head behind stacked plural interveners and a relative clause with its own plural verb
items.passage: Movile Cave in southeastern Romania remained isolated from the surface for millions of years. The primary source of energy for the cave’s dozens of species of spiders, leeches, and other invertebrates, which never encounter sunlight, ______ a floating mat of bacteria that extract energy from hydrogen sulfide dissolved in the groundwater.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “source,” so the singular verb “is” agrees with it. The plural nouns in between (“species,” “spiders,” “leeches,” “invertebrates”) and the plural verb “encounter” belong to the phrase and clause that describe the source.

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present), agrees with the nearest nouns
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “source.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “source.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “source.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Movile Cave, Romania, an ecosystem fed by sulfur-oxidizing bacteria). No named researchers. Band 6: head “source” 22 words before the blank, four plural attractors and a relative clause (which never encounter sunlight) whose own verb is plural; the complement “a floating mat” is singular so “is” reads cleanly.

band7.why: Meets the section 5 R1 settings: four plural attractors, a relative clause with its own plural verb (encounter), head 22 words before the blank, as in 0fe5ce68. Written to band 6; singular head is the weaker direction, but it reads band 7.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb after a dash-enclosed participial interrupter
items.passage: For centuries, residents of the Egyptian town of Oxyrhynchus discarded unwanted documents on rubbish mounds at the desert’s edge, where the arid climate preserved them. Those mounds—excavated by British scholars Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt beginning in 1896—______ hundreds of thousands of papyrus fragments, including lost poems by Sappho.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Those mounds” still needs a main verb when the interruption between the dashes ends. The finite verb “yielded” supplies it, completing the sentence.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: The participle “yielding” leaves “Those mounds” without a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having yielded” is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence remains a fragment.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to yield” cannot serve as the main verb of “Those mounds,” so the sentence is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: history (the Oxyrhynchus rubbish mounds, excavated by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896). Real, well-known facts only. Band 6 on the 3.13 pattern: the dash pair holds a past participle (excavated) that can pass for the main verb, and the blank sits 15 words after its subject.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on the 3.13 pattern with a dash interrupter holding a past participle.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, third verb of a compound predicate after a dash interrupter with its own finite verb
items.passage: Egyptian writer Taha Hussein lost his sight in early childhood, studied at Cairo’s al-Azhar University and subsequently in France, and, in his autobiography The Days—a book whose first volume appeared in the 1920s—______ his village upbringing in the third person, as though writing about someone else.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Taha Hussein” has a series of past-tense verbs joined by “and”: “lost,” “studied,” and a third verb that the blank must supply. The finite past-tense verb “described” completes the series.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: After “and,” the series needs a third past-tense verb to match “lost” and “studied”; the participle “describing” leaves it incomplete.

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to describe” cannot complete a series of finite verbs, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having described” is a participle, not a finite verb, so it cannot be the third verb in the series.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Taha Hussein, The Days, told in the third person). Band 6 as WAVE.md directs: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items, so the planned band 7 is written as a strong band 6. Moves: the blank is the third verb of a series begun 25 words earlier, and the dash interrupter holds its own finite verb (appeared) right before the blank, as the praised clause does in 2.1.

band7.why: R2_finite_second has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 with the blank as the third verb of a series begun 25 words earlier and a finite verb inside the dash interrupter.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical-verb options; singular head behind a title gloss and an appositive with plural nouns
items.passage: Nubian musician Hamza El Din spent his childhood in a village later submerged beneath the reservoir of Egypt’s Aswan High Dam. The title composition of Escalay (The Water Wheel), one of several albums he recorded on the oud, ______ the steady, creaking rhythm of the ox-driven waterwheels that once irrigated Nubian farmland.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “composition,” so the singular verb “captures” agrees with it. The plural noun “albums” in the appositive describes the album Escalay, not the subject.

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present)
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “capture” does not agree with the singular subject “composition.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are capturing” does not agree with the singular subject “composition.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have captured” does not agree with the singular subject “composition.”

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (Hamza El Din’s 1971 oud album Escalay and the Nubian water wheel). Medium: head “composition” 14 words before the blank, with plural “albums” in the appositive as the attractor.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid, singular possessor and plural possessed noun
items.passage: Bayanihan, a Filipino tradition of communal cooperation, is often captured in one striking image: a house in motion. When a family relocates, dozens of the ______ hoist its entire house onto sturdy bamboo poles and transport the structure to a new location.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The neighbors belong to one family (“a family relocates” and “its house”), so the singular possessive “family’s” is needed. “Neighbors” is a plain plural (dozens of them) that owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Neighbor’s” is a possessive, but the neighbors do not own anything in the sentence; the plain plural “neighbors” is needed.

B.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor, wrong possessor number
B.why_wrong: “Families” has no apostrophe to show possession and is plural, though the text describes a single family.

C.why_wrong: “Families’” is a plural possessive, but only one family is relocating (“a family,” “its house”).

items.notes: Subject: social science, Filipino culture (bayanihan, neighbors carrying a family’s house on bamboo poles). Number cues: “a family” before the blank and “its house” after it; “dozens of” for the plural neighbors.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In jotting down), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Essays in Idleness (Tsurezuregusa), composed in Japan around 1330 by the Buddhist monk Yoshida Kenkō, ranges over subjects from friendship to the beauty of impermanence. In jotting down observations on whatever came to mind, ______ in a loose, wandering style that later Japanese essayists would imitate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the observations of Kenkō were recorded
items.explanation: A person is the one who jots down observations. Choice A places “Kenkō” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the writer.

B.why_wrong: The head of “Kenkō’s essays” is “essays,” so the sentence illogically says the essays jotted down observations.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a logical noun to describe.

D.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
D.why_wrong: “The observations” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the observations jotted themselves down.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Yoshida Kenkō’s Essays in Idleness, about 1330). Medium: short, clear opener describing a person; recipes P, E, V.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options; singular head behind a relative clause with a plural subject and verb
items.passage: Builders in Yemen’s Hadhramaut valley have constructed homes from sun-dried mud brick for centuries. The walled city of Shibam, whose approximately 500 tower houses reach heights of up to eleven stories, ______ frequently described as “the Manhattan of the desert.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “city,” so the singular verb “is” agrees with it. The plural “tower houses” and its verb “reach” belong to the clause that describes the city.

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present), agrees with the nearest noun
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “city.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “city.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “city.”

items.notes: Subject: history and architecture (Shibam, Yemen, mud-brick tower houses). Medium: a whose-clause with plural “tower houses,” its plural verb “reach” and plural “heights” and “stories” sits between head and blank.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Made up of), mid-sentence blank
items.passage: Tomás Rivera’s experiences growing up in a family of Mexican American migrant farmworkers informed his celebrated 1971 book …And the Earth Did Not Devour Him. Made up of linked short stories and brief vignettes, ______ follows an unnamed boy as he struggles to reconstruct a forgotten year of his life.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Rivera published this book in 1971, and it
the publication of this book by Rivera
items.explanation: Only the book can be made up of short stories and vignettes. Choice B places “this book by Rivera” right after the opening phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the book.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the author
A.why_wrong: “Rivera” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says the writer himself is made up of short stories and vignettes.

C.why_wrong: The head of the subject is “publication,” so the sentence says an event, rather than the book, is made up of stories and follows a boy.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W) after a prepositional phrase
D.why_wrong: The subject of the clause is “Rivera,” so the sentence still says the writer is made up of short stories and vignettes.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Tomás Rivera’s 1971 book of linked stories and vignettes, the lost year). Medium: plain thing as the right subject; recipes W, N, W.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, -ing result phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: After a glass of wine is swirled, droplets gradually accumulate on the interior of the glass and trickle back down. Because alcohol evaporates more quickly than water from the thin film of wine coating the glass, the film’s surface tension increases and draws additional liquid upward, ______ a ridge that eventually collapses into these “tears.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause is already complete (“the film’s surface tension increases and draws additional liquid upward”). The participle “forming” begins a phrase that describes the result of that pull.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (past)
A.why_wrong: “Formed” would be a second main verb after the comma with no subject or conjunction, which is ungrammatical.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (past perfect)
B.why_wrong: “Had formed” is a finite verb with no subject of its own, so it cannot follow the complete clause after a comma.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed (present)
C.why_wrong: “Form” is a finite verb with no subject of its own; after the comma it leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: physical science (tears of wine, the Marangoni effect). No named researchers. Medium on the 2.9 pattern: the result phrase follows a compound predicate (increases and draws).

items.subtype: Tense, simple present for an ongoing, general process
items.passage: Nighttime visitors to the crater of Kawah Ijen, a volcano in East Java, Indonesia, can witness an unusual phenomenon: brilliant blue flames. The volcano continuously ______ sulfurous gases that ignite on contact with oxygen in the atmosphere, producing an electric-blue glow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes something that happens now and on an ongoing basis (“can witness,” “continuously,” “ignite”). The simple present “releases” fits this ongoing process.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: “Had released” places the action before some other past event, but the text describes a present, ongoing process.

C.why_wrong: “Would have released” describes something that did not happen, which conflicts with the visible flames described in the present.

D.why_wrong: “Will have been releasing” refers to a point in the future, but the text describes what the volcano does now.

items.notes: Subject: earth science (Kawah Ijen, blue flames from burning sulfur gases, East Java). No named researchers. Easy: present cues in the same sentence (continuously, ignite).

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement, subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: Economist Sam Peltzman examined US traffic fatality data from before and after federal law began requiring safety equipment such as seat belts in new cars. In a 1975 paper, ______ argued that drivers who felt safer tended to take more risks, offsetting part of the regulations’ intended benefit.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who wrote the 1975 paper is Sam Peltzman, a single man named in the previous sentence. The singular pronoun “he” refers to him.

A.recipe: wrong number pronoun
A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” does not agree with the singular antecedent “Sam Peltzman.”

B.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” does not refer clearly to Peltzman and does not agree with a single person.

D.why_wrong: “Both” refers to two people or things, but only one economist is named.

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (Peltzman 1975, risk compensation after auto safety regulation). Real, well-known claim only. Easy: one named person as the only possible arguer.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement, subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: Cameroonian artist Francis Bebey worked as a radio journalist, a novelist, and a classical guitarist. In the 1970s and early 1980s, ______ recorded experimental songs that combined drum machines and synthesizers with traditional African instruments such as the sanza, a thumb piano.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who recorded the songs is Francis Bebey, a single man named in the previous sentence. The singular pronoun “he” refers to him.

A.recipe: wrong number pronoun
A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” does not agree with the singular antecedent “Francis Bebey.”

C.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” has no plural antecedent and does not agree with a single musician.

D.why_wrong: “Some” refers to an unspecified group, but the text is about one musician.

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (Francis Bebey’s experimental recordings of the 1970s and early 1980s, drum machines and the sanza). Easy: antecedent is the subject of the previous sentence; the nouns between are singular roles.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options; singular head with a short of-phrase, no number clash
items.passage: Established in the fifth century CE in present-day Bihar, India, the monastery of Nalanda ______ one of the most influential centers of Buddhist scholarship in Asia, attracting students and teachers from as far away as China.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “monastery,” and the opening phrase places it in the past. The singular past verb “was” agrees with the subject.

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” does not agree with the singular subject “monastery.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “monastery.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “monastery.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Nalanda, Buddhist center of learning in Bihar). Easy: head “monastery” three words before the blank, with only the singular name “Nalanda” between.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical-verb options; singular head after each, no intervener
items.passage: In the temple town of Nathdwara in Rajasthan, India, artists create pichwais, elaborate cloth paintings displayed behind the temple’s devotional image of the Hindu god Krishna. Each pichwai ______ an episode from Krishna’s life or a celebration from the temple’s religious calendar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Each pichwai” is singular, so the singular verb “shows” agrees with it.

A.recipe: wrong number (plural present)
A.why_wrong: The plural verb “show” does not agree with the singular subject “Each pichwai.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are showing” does not agree with the singular subject “Each pichwai.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have shown” does not agree with the singular subject “Each pichwai.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (pichwai paintings at Nathdwara). Easy: “Each” plus a singular noun right before the blank; the plural “pichwais” sits in the previous sentence.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb after a short participial phrase
items.passage: Giant tube worms, which cluster around hydrothermal vents on the deep seafloor, have no mouth and no digestive system. Instead, bacteria living inside each worm ______ chemicals from the vent water into nutrients that feed their host.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “bacteria” needs a main verb. The finite present-tense verb “convert” supplies it, completing the sentence.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: The participle “converting” leaves “bacteria” without a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

items.subtype: Tense, past perfect for an action completed before a dated past event

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By + -ing), passage-final blank; the agent is the right subject

the lake’s former bed became some 18,000 hectares of farmland, drained by three steam-powered pumping stations.
the conversion of the lake’s bed into some 18,000 hectares of farmland was achieved by three steam-powered pumping stations.
it was three steam-powered pumping stations that turned the lake’s bed into some 18,000 hectares of farmland.

B.why_wrong: “The lake’s former bed” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the lake bed pumped the water out of the lake.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the conversion,” so the sentence illogically says that a conversion pumped the water out of the lake.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: draining of the Haarlemmermeer, 1849 to 1852 (history of engineering). No named people. Band 6 as 188f7e3c (3.18): plain agent key, recipes W, N, E; key the shortest option.

band7.why: Target band 6, built on 188f7e3c: plain agent key after a By + gerund opener, foils W (lake bed), N (passive nominal) and E (it-cleft, dead per CB 2bca654a/dfbf5d33). No property or 'of' key, so not band 7.

when French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed a lens in the 1820s, he made one that
the lens that French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed in the 1820s
it was a lens designed by French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel in the 1820s that

B.why_wrong: The clause beginning with “when” follows the phrase, and the subject of the main clause is “he,” so the sentence illogically says that Fresnel was built from rings of glass prisms.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: the Fresnel lighthouse lens of the 1820s (science, history of technology). Band 6 as b369d54c and f0864217 (3.1): mid-sentence blank, the thing is the right subject and the person who made it is the main wrong subject; recipes W, S, E.

band7.why: Target band 6, as b369d54c: the thing (the lens) is the subject, its designer is the main foil; W, S and E (it-cleft) recipes. Each foil dies on 'Fresnel was not constructed from prisms'.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Relying on one another) with a dash aside, passage-final blank; the right subject is a compound of the two partners
items.passage: Each of the approximately 750 species of fig tree depends on minuscule pollinating wasps that crawl inside its enclosed flowers to deposit their eggs. Relying on one another to reproduce—the wasps breed nowhere else, and the flowers receive pollen from no other insect—______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the fates of figs and their wasps are thought to have been linked for at least 60 million years.
figs and their wasps are thought to have evolved together for at least 60 million years.
the shared evolutionary history of figs and their wasps is thought to span at least 60 million years.
it is thought that the bond between figs and their wasps has endured for at least 60 million years.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, interrupted by the aside between the dashes, describes things that rely on one another to reproduce: the figs and the wasps. Choice B places “figs and their wasps” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the figs and wasps are the ones relying on each other.

A.recipe: plural 'Y of X' nominal (P): the partners' fates
A.why_wrong: “The fates of figs and their wasps” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that fates rely on one another to reproduce.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the shared evolutionary history,” so the sentence illogically says that a history relies on one another to reproduce.

D.recipe: expletive opener (E), built on another noun
D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: fig trees and their pollinating wasps (science, ecology). No named researchers. Band 7 on 2bca654a (3.21): compound-agent key after an -ing opener with a dash aside.
band7_moves: compound-agent key on the 2bca654a frame: only the two partners together can rely on one another, and every distractor keeps both nouns but places another subject first
hardest distractor (A) starts with “the partnership,” the noun the opener’s idea of mutual reliance seems to describe, and keeps every fact
dash aside inside the opener (as 2bca654a) puts the participle 19 words before the blank; run about 35 words, 15 or more after the blank
the E option is built on another noun (“the bond”), not a cleft wrapped around the key; key is the shortest option

fixes: A changed from the singular "the partnership between figs and their wasps" to the plural "the fates of figs and their wasps": with "one another" requiring a plural subject, B was the only plural option and won on number alone

band7.why: Mirrors band-7 2bca654a: -ing opener with a dash aside, passage-final blank, compound-agent key, E and N foils. After the fix a plural 'of' nominal shares the key's number, so only the modifier logic separates it.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner before its plural antecedent, singular attractors in the previous sentence

items.notes: Subject: male fiddler crabs waving oversized claws (science, animal behavior). No named researchers.
band7_moves: determiner before its antecedent (as 0bcb4417): the owner, “dozens of males,” is the main-clause subject 11 words after the blank

items.notes: Subject: arts, theater (Yakshagana of coastal Karnataka; the bhagavata sings the narration and leads the performance while chande and maddale drummers play). Medium as 2.20 and 2.22: singular head behind an appositive holding a plural noun with its own plural verb (“two drummers keep”).

fixes: options were set / are setting / have set / sets: “set” is also the simple past and fits a singular subject, a second grammatical option; verb changed to dictate (dictate, are dictating, have dictated, dictates)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Instead of + -ing), the agent is the right subject
items.passage: Osmanya, an alphabet devised in the early 1920s by Osman Yusuf Kenadid, was among several writing systems proposed for Somali, a language whose extensive literature had traditionally been transmitted orally. Instead of adopting Osmanya, however, ______ in 1972.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the Somali government made the Latin alphabet the official script for the language
the Latin alphabet was made the official script for the language by the Somali government
the Somali government’s choice for the language’s official script was the Latin alphabet
there was a decision by the Somali government to make the Latin alphabet official
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes someone who chose not to adopt Osmanya. Choice A places “the Somali government” right after the phrase, making clear that the government passed over Osmanya and made the Latin alphabet official instead.

B.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
B.why_wrong: “The Latin alphabet” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the alphabet chose not to adopt Osmanya.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “choice,” not the government, so the sentence illogically says that a choice declined to adopt Osmanya.

D.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: social science, linguistics and language policy (Osmanya, the Somali script created by Osman Yusuf Kenadid around 1920 to 1922; in 1972 the Somali government adopted a Latin-based alphabet instead). Medium as 2.17 and 2.2: short preposition + gerund opener, agent key; recipes V, P, E.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun with a plural attractor just before it
items.passage: Published in 1938, Daniel Olorunfemi Fagunwa’s first novel was among the earliest book-length works of fiction written in the Yoruba language. In 1968, Nigerian playwright Wole Soyinka translated the novel, which follows a hunter’s adventures through a forest inhabited by supernatural creatures, into English, giving ______ the title The Forest of a Thousand Daemons.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the novel, which Soyinka gave an English title. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with the singular antecedent “the novel.”

A.recipe: wrong number pronoun
A.why_wrong: The plural “them” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “the novel”; the nearby plural “creatures” is not what received the title.

B.why_wrong: The plural demonstrative “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “the novel.”

D.why_wrong: The pronoun “one” is unclear in this context; the resulting sentence doesn’t make clear what Soyinka gave the title to.

items.notes: Subject: literature (D. O. Fagunwa's 1938 Yoruba novel Ògbójú Ọdẹ nínú Igbó Irúnmọlẹ̀, translated by Wole Soyinka in 1968 as The Forest of a Thousand Daemons; the Yoruba title is left out so the antecedent is plainly “the novel”). Medium as 2.15: the plural attractor (“supernatural creatures”) sits just before the pronoun, inside a relative clause that interrupts the main clause.

fixes: option D “this” could be defended for a specific thing (CB 42cc9236 rationale); replaced with “one”, as in model 2.15

items.subtype: Simple past for a dated past action reported in a present-tense frame (“Historians note that ...”)
items.passage: In late 1872, Japan’s government suddenly replaced the country’s traditional lunisolar calendar with the Gregorian calendar. Historians note that officials ______ the change partly to save money: under the old calendar, 1873 would have had a thirteenth month, and government workers would have expected an extra month’s pay.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The change took place in late 1872, so the verb describing what officials did must be in the past tense. The simple past “timed” fits this completed past action.

A.recipe: present perfect for a dated past event
A.why_wrong: The present perfect “have timed” doesn’t fit an action completed at a specific past time, late 1872.

C.recipe: future for a dated past event
C.why_wrong: The future “will time” doesn’t fit an action that took place in 1872.

D.why_wrong: “Are timing” describes an action in progress now, not a decision made in 1872.

items.notes: Subject: history (Japan's switch from the lunisolar to the Gregorian calendar at the end of 1872, which spared the government a thirteenth month of salaries in 1873). Medium as 2.12: a dated past event in the first sentence, then “Historians note that officials ______”; foils present perfect, future and present progressive. The “would have” clauses are counterfactual and don't bear on the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement in a relative clause: singular antecedent, plural nouns elsewhere
items.passage: Moist air flowing over a mountain range can oscillate in a series of atmospheric waves on the range’s downwind side. Near the crest of a wave, the air may cool sufficiently to produce a lenticular cloud, a smooth, lens-shaped formation that ______ stationary for hours even as powerful winds blow through it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank is the verb of the clause beginning with “that,” which refers to the singular noun “formation” (the lenticular cloud). The singular verb “remains” agrees with “formation.”

A.recipe: wrong number, present
A.why_wrong: “Remain” is plural, but “that” refers to the singular “formation,” not to “waves” or “winds.”

B.why_wrong: “Have remained” is plural and doesn’t agree with “formation.”

C.why_wrong: “Are remaining” is plural and doesn’t agree with “formation.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, meteorology (lenticular clouds forming at the crests of lee waves downwind of mountains and staying in place while wind blows through them). Medium as 2.18: the blank is the verb of a relative clause; plural nouns elsewhere (“waves,” “winds”) are the attractors.

items.subtype: Simple present for a general fact
items.passage: Graupel, sometimes called soft hail, forms when a falling snowflake passes through a cloud of supercooled water droplets, which freeze onto its surface. Unlike genuine hailstones, which are dense and hard, graupel ______ easily when it is squeezed between two fingers, and it rarely causes the destruction associated with hailstorms.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The text describes what graupel generally does, using present-tense verbs such as “forms,” “are,” and “causes.” The simple present “crumbles” fits this general description.

B.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Crumbled” refers to a single past event, not to what graupel generally does.

C.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
C.why_wrong: “Had crumbled” places the action before another past event, but the text states a general fact.

D.why_wrong: “Was crumbling” describes an action in progress in the past, not a general fact.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, meteorology (graupel, snow pellets formed when supercooled droplets freeze onto falling snowflakes; soft and easily crushed, unlike hail). Easy as 1.37 and 1.25: general-present frame with present verbs in both sentences.

items.subtype: Simple present for a habitual action (“Each spring”)
items.passage: In Kyrgyzstan, many herding families maintain a seasonal routine that is centuries old. Each spring, as snow melts in the surrounding mountains, these families ______ their livestock to high-altitude summer pastures known as jailoo, where they live in traditional yurts until autumn.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “Each spring” and the present-tense verbs “maintain,” “melts,” and “live” show that the text describes a repeated, current practice. The simple present “drive” fits.

A.recipe: simple past where the present is needed
A.why_wrong: “Drove” places the action in the past, but the text describes a yearly practice that continues today.

B.recipe: past perfect where the present is needed
B.why_wrong: “Had driven” places the action before another past event, which the text doesn’t describe.

D.why_wrong: “Were driving” describes an ongoing past action, not a repeated present one.

items.notes: Subject: social science, anthropology (Kyrgyz seasonal migration of herds to high summer pastures called jailoo, where families live in yurts). Easy as 1.17: “Each spring” plus present verbs before and after the blank.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: object pronoun, singular antecedent
items.passage: Sous-verre, or reverse glass painting, has been particularly popular in Senegal since the early twentieth century. Because a sous-verre image is intended to be viewed through the glass on which it is painted, an artist must paint ______ in reverse order, beginning with intricate details and finishing with the background.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a sous-verre image,” the thing the artist paints. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with this singular antecedent.

A.recipe: wrong number pronoun
A.why_wrong: The plural “them” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “a sous-verre image.”

B.why_wrong: The plural “these” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “a sous-verre image.”

C.why_wrong: The plural “those” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “a sous-verre image.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Senegalese sous-verre, reverse glass painting popular since the early twentieth century; details are painted first and the background last). Easy as 1.19 and 1.12: object pronoun, one singular antecedent in the same sentence, wrong-number demonstratives as foils.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family options: singular head (a title) behind a short participial phrase
items.passage: In the early 1300s, Persian statesman Rashid al-Din served as chief minister to the Mongol rulers of Iran. His Compendium of Chronicles, completed around 1310, ______ one of the most ambitious early attempts to write a comprehensive history of the known world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “Compendium” (the title of a single work), so the verb must be singular. The singular verb “is” agrees with it.

A.recipe: wrong number, present
A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural; “Chronicles” is part of the title, not the head of the subject, “Compendium.”

C.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Compendium.”

D.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Compendium.”

items.notes: Subject: history (Rashid al-Din, vizier of the Ilkhanate, and his Jami' al-tawarikh, the Compendium of Chronicles, completed about 1307 to 1310). Easy as 1.4 and 1.38: singular head with a short participial interrupter; the title's plural “Chronicles” is the only attractor.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: singular head behind a participial phrase
items.passage: Papakōlea Beach, located near the southern tip of Hawaii’s Big Island, ______ its distinctive olive-green color from olivine, a mineral that erodes from an old volcanic cone next to the shoreline. Because olivine crystals are comparatively dense, waves gradually carry lighter sand particles away while leaving the green crystals behind.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the singular noun “Papakōlea Beach,” so the verb must be singular. The singular verb “gets” agrees with it.

B.why_wrong: “Get” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Papakōlea Beach.”

C.why_wrong: “Are getting” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Papakōlea Beach.”

D.why_wrong: “Have gotten” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Papakōlea Beach.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science, geology (Papakōlea green sand beach near South Point, Hawaii, colored by olivine eroded from a nearby cinder cone; the dense grains stay while lighter sand washes away). Easy as 1.20: singular head behind a participial phrase with no plural noun.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, lexical verb: named singular subject right before the blank
items.passage: Chilean writer María Luisa Bombal’s 1938 novel The Shrouded Woman (La amortajada) has an unusual narrator: Ana María, a woman who has just died. Lying in her coffin, Ana María ______ the relatives and former lovers who attend her funeral vigil, recalling her complicated relationship with each of them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “Ana María,” a single person, so the verb must be singular. The singular verb “observes” agrees with it.

A.recipe: wrong number, present
A.why_wrong: “Observe” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Ana María.”

B.why_wrong: “Are observing” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Ana María.”

C.why_wrong: “Have observed” is plural and doesn’t agree with “Ana María.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (María Luisa Bombal's La amortajada, 1938, narrated by a woman lying dead at her own wake). Easy as 1.6: a named singular subject right before the blank, plural nouns only after it.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a subject with an appositive
items.passage: Crushing a wintergreen-flavored hard candy in a darkened room produces a brief flash of bluish light. Methyl salicylate, the compound responsible for the candy’s flavor, ______ invisible ultraviolet light from the fracturing sugar crystals into visible light.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence needs a main verb for its subject, “Methyl salicylate.” The finite verb “converts” provides it and completes the sentence.

A.recipe: nonfinite: having + past participle
A.why_wrong: “Having converted” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

B.why_wrong: “Converting” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

D.why_wrong: “To convert” is not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, chemistry and physics (triboluminescence of wintergreen candy: breaking sugar crystals give off ultraviolet light that methyl salicylate turns into visible blue light). Easy as 1.21 and 1.30: main verb after a subject with an appositive.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive: singular possessor + plural noun, two-slot grid
items.passage: Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, composed his memoir, the Baburnama, in Chagatai, a Turkic language. Many of the ______ offer detailed descriptions of the vegetation, wildlife, and customs of India, which Babur frequently compared unfavorably with those of his homeland in Central Asia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passages belong to one memoir, so the singular possessive “memoir’s” is needed, and “passages” is a plain plural noun (“Many of the”), so it takes no apostrophe.

A.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor
A.why_wrong: “Memoirs” lacks the apostrophe that shows the passages belong to the memoir.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Passage’s” is possessive, but the noun here is simply plural.

D.why_wrong: “Memoirs’” is a plural possessive, but Babur wrote one memoir.

items.notes: Subject: literature, history (Babur's memoir, the Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic, with long descriptions of India's plants, animals and customs, often compared unfavorably with his Central Asian homeland). Easy as 1.16 and 1.36: possessor x plural grid; number cues “his memoir” and “Many of the.”

items.subtype: Past perfect for a state lasting up to a past point (“By the time ... died”)
items.passage: Eyak, a language historically spoken along the Copper River delta in southern Alaska, lost its last native speaker in 2008, after decades of documentation by linguists. By the time Marie Smith Jones died that year, she ______ the only remaining fluent speaker of Eyak for more than a decade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “By the time Marie Smith Jones died that year” sets a point in the past, and the blank describes a situation that lasted up to that point. The past perfect “had been” shows this.

A.recipe: present simple
A.why_wrong: The present tense “is” doesn’t fit a situation that ended with her death in 2008.

B.why_wrong: The future “will be” doesn’t fit a situation that ended in 2008.

C.why_wrong: “Has been” describes a situation continuing to the present, but this one ended with her death in 2008.

items.notes: Subject: social science, linguistics (Eyak, Copper River delta, Alaska; Marie Smith Jones, its last native speaker, died in 2008, her sister having died in the mid-1990s). Easy as 1.24: an explicit earlier-than-past frame (“By the time ... died that year”); no simple past is offered, so no second defensible option.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a complete clause
items.passage: Bermuda has no rivers or freshwater lakes, so its residents have long depended on rainfall for drinking water. Builders there traditionally give houses white, stepped limestone roofs ______ rainwater into storage tanks constructed beneath each building.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first part of the sentence (“Builders there traditionally give houses white, stepped limestone roofs”) is already a complete clause. The infinitive “to channel” begins a phrase that explains the purpose of the roofs.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: “Channeled” adds a second main verb with no conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: “Channels” adds a second main verb with no conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
D.why_wrong: “Are channeling” adds a second main verb with no conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: engineering, architecture (Bermuda's white stepped limestone roofs channel rain into tanks beneath houses; the island has no rivers or lakes). Easy as 1.22 and 1.27: purpose infinitive after a complete clause; three finite foils only, so no -ing form can read as an acceptable participial phrase.

fixes: explanation quotes the clause in full instead of with an ellipsis

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate
items.passage: Drapo Vodou, the sequined flags displayed during Haitian Vodou ceremonies, often depict spirits or their symbols. To create one, an artist sketches a design on a piece of satin and ______ thousands of sequins and glass beads along its outlines, attaching them individually.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank follows “and,” so it holds the second verb of a compound predicate that begins “an artist sketches a design on a piece of satin.” The finite present-tense verb “sews” matches “sketches” and completes the sentence.

A.recipe: nonfinite: to have + past participle
A.why_wrong: “To have sewn” is not a finite verb, so it can’t pair with “sketches” as a second main verb.

C.why_wrong: “Sewing” is not a finite verb, so it can’t pair with “sketches” as a second main verb.

D.why_wrong: “To sew” is not a finite verb, so it can’t pair with “sketches” as a second main verb.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Haitian drapo Vodou, sequined and beaded ceremonial flags on satin depicting spirits or their symbols). Easy as 1.11: second verb of a compound predicate after “and,” with 1.11's distractor set and the tense moved to the present.

fixes: explanation quotes the passage in full instead of with an ellipsis

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing result phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: In 2009, a group of entrepreneurs in Sardinia, Italy, launched Sardex, a complementary currency that member businesses can spend only with one another. The participating firms buy goods and services from each other using Sardex credits rather than euros, ______ them to keep operating even when cash is scarce.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first part of the sentence is a complete clause, so the blank must begin a phrase that adds a result rather than a new clause. The participle “allowing” does this correctly.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
A.why_wrong: “Allows” adds a second main verb with no subject or conjunction, making the sentence ungrammatical.

B.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
B.why_wrong: “It allows” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma.

D.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
D.why_wrong: “This will allow” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (Sardex, a mutual-credit currency launched in Sardinia in 2009 that member businesses spend only with one another). Easy as 1.29: result phrase after a complete clause, two pronoun + finite comma-splice foils and one bare finite form.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (In addition to + -ing), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is a possessive noun phrase built on the obvious noun
items.passage: Elephants can coordinate their movements with members of their herd that are several kilometers away and out of sight. In addition to traveling through the air, ______ which other elephants appear to detect through sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: elephants send their low-pitched rumbles through the ground as vibrations,
elephants’ low-pitched rumbles pass through the ground as vibrations,
the passage of elephants’ low-pitched rumbles through the ground creates vibrations,
there are low-pitched rumbles from elephants that pass through the ground as vibrations,
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that travels through the air. Choice B places “elephants’ low-pitched rumbles” right after the phrase, making clear that the rumbles, not the elephants themselves, travel through the air and also pass through the ground as vibrations.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun
A.why_wrong: “Elephants” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the elephants themselves travel through the air.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the passage,” so the sentence illogically says that a passage travels through the air.

D.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there are,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (elephants send low-frequency rumbles through the ground as seismic vibrations that other elephants sense through their feet; no researchers named). Band-7 moves from spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md section 3 (7) and section 5: the opener describes a property of the animal, so the right subject is the possessive noun phrase “elephants’ low-pitched rumbles” and the obvious noun, “elephants” (the topic of sentence 1, which never mentions rumbles), is the trap (W). Recipes W, N, E, as in 37e5c794 (E, W, P) and 2dd1b8bf. Mid-sentence blank: each option ends in “vibrations,” and joins the relative clause after it. Each option read in the full sentence: only B leaves no dangling modifier.

review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: Move 7: the opener describes a property, so the right subject is the possessive phrase “elephants’ low-pitched rumbles” built on the obvious noun; the trap A keeps every fact with “elephants” as subject (W), as in 2dd1b8bf and 37e5c794; mid-sentence blank with 14 words after it, run about 32 words.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener, passage-final blank; the right subject is the work (possessive noun phrase), not the artist
items.passage: Senegalese artist Ousmane Sow practiced physical therapy for some twenty years before devoting himself to sculpture in the 1980s. Standing far taller than a person and depicting wrestlers, warriors, and herders from several African peoples, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Sow drew some three million visitors when he displayed his figures on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
some three million visitors came to see Sow’s figures when they were displayed on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
Sow’s figures drew some three million visitors when they were displayed on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
there were some three million visitors to Sow’s figures when they were displayed on a bridge in Paris in 1999.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes things that stand far taller than a person and depict wrestlers, warriors, and herders. Choice C places “Sow’s figures” right after the phrase, making clear that the sculptures, not the artist or the visitors, are what the phrase describes.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun
A.why_wrong: “Sow” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the artist himself stood far taller than a person.

B.why_wrong: “Some three million visitors” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the visitors stood far taller than a person and depicted wrestlers and warriors.

D.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there were,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Ousmane Sow, Senegalese sculptor and former physical therapist; his larger-than-life figures shown on the Pont des Arts in Paris in 1999 drew about three million visitors; known, real). Band-7 moves: the right subject is the possessive noun phrase “Sow’s figures” built on the obvious noun, the artist, who is the trap (W); “depicting” could describe an artist, so only “Standing far taller than a person” rules Sow out, a two-part check. Passage-final, as 2bca654a and dab8b8ee; recipes W, W, E (reviewer replaced the nominalised “the display of Sow’s figures,” since an exhibit can itself stand tall and depict figures). Options 15 to 19 words, all carrying the same facts.

fixes: D: replaced “the display of Sow’s figures ...” (a display can stand tall and depict, so defensible) with an expletive “there were ...” option
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: Move 7: the right subject “Sow’s figures” is built on the obvious noun, the artist; “depicting” fits Sow, so only “Standing far taller than a person” rules A out; sentence-final blank like its band-7 model 2bca654a; options carry the same facts. Weak D (a display can stand tall and depict) replaced by an expletive.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener, mid-sentence blank; the right subject is the epic, not the historian or the readers
items.passage: For centuries, griots—hereditary oral historians and musicians of West Africa—have preserved the story of Sundiata Keita, the thirteenth-century founder of the Mali Empire. A narrative of exile, return, and military conquest, ______ in 1960, when it appeared in a French prose adaptation based on the recitation of a Guinean griot.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the epic of Sundiata reached a wide audience of readers
historian Djibril Tamsir Niane brought the epic of Sundiata to many readers
a wide audience of readers first encountered the epic of Sundiata
there was a wide audience of readers for the epic of Sundiata
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a story: a narrative of exile, return, and military conquest. Choice A places “the epic of Sundiata” right after the phrase, making clear that the epic is the narrative the phrase describes.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): a person
B.why_wrong: “Historian Djibril Tamsir Niane” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the historian is a narrative of exile, return, and military conquest.

C.why_wrong: “A wide audience of readers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the readers are a narrative of exile, return, and military conquest.

D.why_wrong: The phrase is followed by “there was,” which leaves the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: literature (the Sundiata epic of the griots, put into French prose by D. T. Niane in 1960 from the recitation of a Guinean griot, Mamadou Kouyaté; real, known). R3_appositive has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/form_structure_and_sense.md appendix), and the plan sets band 6: a strong band 6. Mid-sentence blank like 5b8f9cf2 and e060dd6b: options end so the clause continues with “in 1960, when it appeared ...”. Recipes W (person), W (readers), E. Each option read in the full sentence; only A leaves no dangling modifier.

fixes: D: replaced the it-cleft (“it” could refer to “the story of Sundiata Keita,” a narrative, so defensible) with an expletive “there was ...” option
review.options_tested: each option read in the full sentence; only the key is standard

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; it is a strong band 6 on 5b8f9cf2 and e060dd6b (mid-sentence blank, three W/E distractors that keep every fact).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, plural head behind singular nouns and a relative clause with its own singular verb

items.passage: Cuban poet Nicolás Guillén published Motivos de son, a collection of eight short poems, in 1930. In these poems, Guillén reproduced the vernacular speech of working-class Black residents of Havana and ______ the syncopated rhythms of son, a popular Afro-Cuban musical genre.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank holds the second verb of a compound predicate: Guillén “reproduced” the speech of Havana’s residents “and” echoed the rhythms of son. The finite past-tense verb “echoed” matches “reproduced.”

A.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
A.why_wrong: The nonfinite “echoing” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “reproduced.”

C.recipe: to + base where a finite verb is needed
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to echo” can’t serve as the second verb of the predicate that begins with “reproduced.”

D.recipe: having + past participle where a finite verb is needed
D.why_wrong: The nonfinite “having echoed” can’t be joined by “and” to the finite verb “reproduced.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (Nicolás Guillén’s Motivos de son, 1930, eight poems in Afro-Cuban vernacular modeled on son; real, known). Easy as 1.11: “reproduced ... and ______” with the canonical nonfinite distractors.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite, -ing participial phrase after a complete clause
items.passage: Lugworms inhabit U-shaped burrows in the sandy shores and mudflats along the coasts of the North Atlantic. The worms continually ingest sediment and digest the bacteria and other microorganisms coating its grains, ______ distinctive coiled casts of processed sand at the surface beside each burrow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “The worms continually ingest sediment and digest the bacteria and other microorganisms coating its grains” is complete, so the blank must begin a phrase that describes a result. The participle “leaving” does this without creating a second independent clause.

A.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
A.why_wrong: “This leaves” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “leaves” has no subject of its own here and doesn’t agree with “The worms,” so it can’t follow the comma.

D.recipe: comma splice via pronoun + finite verb
D.why_wrong: “They leave” creates a second independent clause joined to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (lugworms of North Atlantic shores swallow sediment, digest the microorganisms on it and leave coiled casts; real, known). Easy as 1.29: a result phrase after a complete clause, with two comma-splice options and a bare finite form.
